title: Why The Cabin Lights Go Down Before Landing

scenes.narration: The cabin lights go down before a night landing, and it reads as mood lighting or saving power.
scenes.note: Two wrong explanations offered up front, both of which the viewer probably holds.

beats.action: the cabin dims for landing; window shades up, night outside
the lights fade; a MOOD LIGHTING label appears
a SAVING POWER label appears beside it
the cabin dims another step; the window darkens

scenes.note: One beat. Both labels die together.

beats.action: both labels cross out at once

scenes.narration: Eyes take several minutes to adapt to darkness, and takeoff and landing are when an evacuation is most likely to be needed.
scenes.note: Dark adaptation as a timed process. The clock matters — minutes, not instants.

beats.action: an eye diagram in bright light, pupil small
the light drops; the pupil widens slowly against a running clock
takeoff and landing highlight on a flight profile as the risk windows
the pupil widens further as the clock runs on
beats.sync: secondary action — closes a pacing gap

scenes.narration: If the cabin were brightly lit and the power went, everyone aboard would be effectively blind at the worst possible moment.
scenes.note: The counterfactual, stated calmly. Bright then dark, and nobody can see. No screaming, no fire.

beats.action: a brightly lit cabin in cross-section, everything clearly visible
the lights cut; the frame goes near-black
the exits are unreadable in the dark; a clock ticks off the adaptation delay

scenes.narration: Dimming early means your eyes are already adjusted, and the floor path lighting reads clearly instead of washing out. The lights go down so you can see.
scenes.note: The resolution: pre-adapted eyes read the cabin instantly. End on the floor lighting.

the floor path lighting and exit signs read clearly and brightly
the exit path glows the full length of the aisle; hard cut
the exit signs brighten against the dim cabin
